## Introduction

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPVs act more like normal skin flora than disease-causing pathogens. They are acquired early in life, are ubiquitous in healthy adults, and persist as asymptomatic, low-level infections [@antonsson2000; @doorbar2023] that expand when host immunity fails [@hou2026]. At the DNA level, this viral reservoir is large and well mapped. Shotgun metagenomics detected HPV in 61.3% of healthy skin samples [@ma2014], and skin swabs found beta-HPV in 92% of adults [@rollison2019sites]. The community is highly diverse, spanning 396 distinct types, 229 of which were previously unknown [@bzhalava2014]. However, DNA detection alone cannot show whether any of these viral genomes are transcribed.

Understanding this is critical because beta-HPV is a suspected cofactor in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), particularly among organ transplant recipients [@howley2015; @rollison2019]. Three distinct, mutually compatible theories account for this role using the same underlying evidence. Under the "hit-and-run" model, beta-HPV acts synergistically with ultraviolet radiation, immunosuppression, or chronic inflammation during early tumorigenesis, but becomes dispensable once the tumor is established [@viarisio2018; @dorfer2021]. Crucially, this model proposes only that the virus is no longer required, not that it is actively cleared, so viral activity declines only where a mechanism for viral loss exists. For instance, ultraviolet-induced mutations in *TP53* or *NOTCH* can render viral oncogenes redundant, removing the selective pressure to maintain the viral genome [@viarisio2018]. Alternatively, the protective-immunity model proposes that T-cell responses against commensal papillomaviruses actively suppress skin carcinogenesis, so viral loss reflects immune-mediated selection rather than dispensability [@strickley2019; @lambert2021; @strickley2021]. Recent evidence supports this: viral colonization restricts the expansion of p53-mutant clones, and beta-HPV is progressively lost as those clones outgrow [@son2025]. A third model requires neither premise: transcriptional silence is the viral default, because the beta-HPV genome uses E8\^E2 to autorepress its own expression, and transformation requires inactivating this repressor [@rehm2022]. All three models therefore predict declining viral activity from healthy skin to carcinoma, so measuring that decline more precisely cannot distinguish among them.

Studies directly testing whether HPV is transcribed in cSCC have mostly found little or no viral transcription. The original cSCC transcriptome study detected no viral transcripts [@arron2011], nor did an analysis of 12 skin lesions at a median depth of 66 million reads [@hultin2019]. A study of 345 posttransplant tumors at 35 million reads identified transcription in only 15 cases [@arroyomuhr2021], and 23 risk-stratified biopsies showed none despite a 64% DNA positivity rate [@vandiver2021]. E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization showed expression in just 0.9% of 225 nonanogenital cSCCs [@fujimoto2019]. The literature is not unanimous: in situ hybridization detected epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV)-associated HPV transcripts in 4 of 11 PCR-positive transplant cSCCs [@purdie2005]. These studies share several limitations. Most examined lesions in isolation, so they cannot establish how often HPV is transcribed in carcinoma relative to healthy skin. Sample sizes were modest, from 11 to 345 specimens, four of the five lacked a comparison group of unselected skin, the largest cohort was restricted to formalin-fixed transplant tissue, and none assessed productive viral replication.

Public sequencing archives make such a large-scale comparison possible. Standard RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) pipelines align reads to the human reference genome and discard unmapped reads. Viral reads go with them, but remain in the raw data deposited in public repositories and can be recovered by targeted reanalysis [@edgar2022]. The strategy has already been applied to skin datasets [@leiendecker2023; @bhargava2025], but carries notable technical pitfalls: HeLa-derived HPV18 extensively contaminates archived sequencing data [@cantalupo2015; @kazemian2015; @adey2013], and sequencing depth and library chemistry constrain detection sensitivity. Here, we reanalyzed public human RNA-seq data spanning healthy skin, warts, and skin cancer to determine how often cutaneous HPV is transcribed, which types are present, and whether these infections are productive.
